EAW BRANCH SUPPLEMENT

AN APPRECIATION
from MISS MARY GEORGE

AS this is the last occasion when I shall be contributing to The Electrical Age as EAW Director I do want to say how much I have valued the contact I have had with readers through my regular articles. All big organisations need a journal or bulletin as a means of disseminating news and information to all those concerned with their activities.

Earlier on in Germany, as a member of a local
British relief committee, I used to visit three
camps for displaced persons in the Oldenburg
area. One of these, Varel, was a former German
barracks housing men and women from eleven
different countries together in their national
groups. It was fascinating to see how the women,
in their roles as home makers, managed — even
in such unlikely surroundings and with a bare
minimum of materials — to build up the domes-
tic atmosphere of their own homelands.

A Family Story from 1825

by IAN RITCHIE

FIFTY years ago, when other communities in and around the Vale of Avalon had their main thoroughfares lit by gaslight, Street — a Somerset village in which two Quaker brothers, Cyrus and James Clark, had established a shoe-making business a hundred years before that — was brilliantly lit by electricity. This was entirely due to the fact that the Clark family, who have been pioneers in numerous technical and educational innovations, bought the first dynamo for generating power at their factory in 1911.

article_title: Advertisement: British Egg Information Service - Eggs in Action: 8 QUICHES
brief_extract:
Eggs in Action: 8
QUICHES

QUICHES are rich egg custard tarts, baked in a shallow pastry case with savoury or sweet ingredients added and served hot or cold. The best known quiche originated in the Lorraine region of France with bread dough used as a base. EGGS are used whole or sometimes with whole egg and yolks combined making a richer custard and reducing liquid content.

brief_extract:
Bullfinches are very partial to gooseberry buds
and one pair can seriously affect the cropping
of plums and cherries. They are such a menace
in the orchards in Kent that many growers have
been forced to grub up their cherry orchards and
plant apples. Apples suffer from so many pests and diseases
that it will be necessary to consult 'The Fruit
Garden Displayed'.

Plants in containers
Last year my wife and I spent our summer
holiday in France. There seem to be few gardens
outside town and village houses that compare
with our own.

brief_context: Mentioned as having an increasing interest in container gardening.
brief_extract:
But where they do excel is growing
plants in pots and window boxes. There seems
to be an increasing interest in this sort of garden-
ing in Britain and so, perhaps, a few words on the
subject would be useful. There is a wide choice of containers and a visit
to your local garden centre would help you to
decide if it is a trough, pot or window box that
best suits your needs or pockets.

brief_context: Geographical area comparison for solar energy collectors.
brief_extract: We must learn to harness more solar energy but this is difficult because it is not very intense. This means that to generate two thousand million watts, the output of a modern power station, you would need to collect all the sun's power which fell on 6 thousandths of Greater London. If solar collectors collect one-third of the sun's power, you would have to cover one fiftieth of Greater London, but the modern power station covers less than one thousandth of London's area and most of it is in fact grass, fuel storage or cooling water.

brief_context: Reference to industrial energy usage in the country.
brief_extract:
Therefore, harnessing the sun's energy directly is difficult, requiring massive engineering schemes and new technologies, taking time and energy. Saving Energy Now
Industry uses almost half of our energy in the UK, and our homes, schools and offices consume another third. Consideration must be given to four main principles: removal of inbuilt obsolescence; reduction of waste heat; reduction of waste material; and recovery of the energy we waste.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding energy consumption in the iron and steel industry.
brief_extract: Articles are made in several separate stages and in general the more stages used the more energy is wasted. The iron and steel industry accounts for one-fifth of the energy consumed in the UK but the layout of existing factories wastes heat and mechanical energy. New integrated factories are being built where all the energy consuming stages of manufacture are collected together to provide for continuous casting, but we have to improve the efficiency of heating and cooling in existing factories.

brief_context: Location of the Electricity Council where energy efficiency work occurred.
brief_extract: Conventional coke and oil fired furnaces are very inefficient. A modern gas fired furnace can reduce a lot of waste, but a direct resistance heater developed by the Electricity Council at Capenhurst is more efficient than the alternatives, even taking account of the fact that electricity is itself a manufactured product requiring three units of primary energy to make one unit of electrical energy. The waste of heat energy through warehouse doors open for 8 hours a day and hot air spilling out of shop doorways could be reduced by automatic electrically controlled doors.

location_standardised: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
brief_context: The city where the visitors stayed with Rita.
brief_extract:
Nothing is too much
trouble to do for others. In Port of Spain our
hostess Rita who was not then a member agreed
to take two of our party, a husband and wife,
and, because our designated hostess had
plumbing trouble Rita took the two of us in as
well. She left the house before 7 a.m.

brief_context: Place where the group met the Mayor and Carib royalty.
brief_extract:
She would not let us eat out
immediately before the Carnival since in their
family they had never been allowed out at that
time. A colourful character was the Mayor of Arima
who was very proud of his Carib blood,
indigenous to the island, and as anxious for us
to meet his Carib Queen (and King). We
followed him at the end of an evening reception
but the pair had gone to bed, having expected us
much earlier.

brief_context: Mentioned in relation to visits from U.K. Royalty.
brief_extract:
Being most embarrassed we said
'no' but he insisted. The couple got up, dressed
and graciously shook hands with us all and
chatted away showing us treasured photographs
and recalling visits from U.K. Royalty.

location_standardised: Independence Square, Port of Spain, Trinidad, Trinidad and Tobago
brief_context: Location where cannons were fired during Carnival.
brief_extract: No one walks, everyone dances and one of the most delightful sights was a policeman on point duty directing traffic with one hand while dancing with the rest of his body. A loud blast of cannons from Independence Square at 5 a.m. on the morning of March 1 announces that from then on the streets will be filled with bands, Kings and Queens of the band, and many thousands of followers all in lovely colourful costumes dancing on their way to show themselves off on the enormous stage at the Savannah between the Grandstands and then round and round again.

The annual awards made by the EAW on the results of the Home Electricity Examinations have been won by the groups and individuals throughout the country. Dame Allan's Girls School, Newcastle-on-Tyne won the Councillor Miss Walter Rosebowl for students under 16 1/2 years, and Northumberland County Technical College, Ashington won the Banbury Shield for the runner-up in the over 16 1/2 years age group. In the higher age category the premier award of the Worcester Vase was won by Mid-Essex Technical College, Chelmsford for the second year running.

brief_context: Mentioned as a region where frosts might still occur.
brief_extract:
In Your Garden

by FREDERICK M PROCTER, Electricity Council

THE coming of June is generally a sign that summer has at last begun in earnest. Except for residents in Scotland and Northern England, we have seen the last of frosts for a few months so that it is safe to plant out all the half hardy annuals. You have, no doubt, prepared the beds by forking over the top soil, at the same time incorporating well rotten compost or manure or, if these are not available, garden peat with a general fertiliser at a rate of about 2 oz per sq yd (6g per sq m).

brief_context: Area mentioned for having low winter rainfall.
brief_extract:
Mulching
During long spells of hot weather the local Water Authority is liable to impose restrictions on the use of water. In fact we had so little rain in the South East last winter that the use of water in the garden could well be prohibited. We obviously have to take the necessary action to retain as much soil moisture as possible and one of the most effective ways of doing this is by mulching.

location_standardised: Trentham Gardens, Trentham, Staffordshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Garden on the A34 worth a visit.
brief_extract: If the male members of your family are railway enthusiasts they will be fascinated by the collection of steam locomotives. Trentham Gardens on the A34, 3 miles (5 km) from Stoke-on-Trent has been commercialised but is still worth a visit. My two favourite Scottish gardens are Crathes Castle 14 miles (22 km) west of Aberdeen just north of the A93 on the north bank of the River Dee, and Inverewe in Wester Ross, which was created by the late Osgood Mackenzie; it is noted for the sub-tropical plants.

brief_extract: Trentham Gardens on the A34, 3 miles (5 km) from Stoke-on-Trent has been commercialised but is still worth a visit. My two favourite Scottish gardens are Crathes Castle 14 miles (22 km) west of Aberdeen just north of the A93 on the north bank of the River Dee, and Inverewe in Wester Ross, which was created by the late Osgood Mackenzie; it is noted for the sub-tropical plants. Inverewe is 7 miles (11 km) from Gairloch and 36 miles (52 km) from Achnasheen Station and is well worth making a detour of many miles to see.

brief_extract: On 22nd June, the first day of the great summer heat wave, I accompanied our Chairman, Mrs. Barbara Peirson, to Church House, Westminster where we joined more than 400 delegates, whose presence reflected every kind of specialised knowledge and all shades of opinion relating to the different forms of energy. There were the heads of the energy industries and the heads of their associated unions; the heads of the TUC and the CBI; people from professional, academic and research bodies and people representing consumer, conservation and environmental interests, as well as representatives of social agencies concerned particularly with the underprivileged and the elderly.

article_title: The Way Ahead - from the first National Energy Conference
brief_extract:
The Way Ahead

— from the first National Energy Conference

by ANN McMULLAN
Director EAW

Buckinghamshire Advertiser

THE EAW, as one of four women's organisations invited to participate in the first National Energy Conference convened last June by Mr. Anthony Wedgwood Benn, the Secretary of State for Energy, was pleased at its inclusion in a necessarily limited invitation list, and honoured by this Government recognition of its role in helping to create informed public opinion concerning the domestic uses of electricity in the community.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding energy prospects to the year 2000.
brief_extract:
Each was outlined in a brief agenda, together with suggested areas for decisions, topics for discussion and questions raised in papers submitted in advance of the Conference by the major participants. Scope
The morning session of 2½ hours dealt with the supply and demand for energy; UK prospects to the year 2000; problems and constraints, priorities and possible solutions. Also considered was the role of each energy industry and its problems, plans and decisions.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding energy resources and nuclear energy generation.
brief_extract:
Speakers
Opening the Conference, Mr. James Callaghan, the Prime Minister, made it clear that Britain's considerable energy resources would be used to revitalise the country's industries. Current estimates, he said, put the gross value of oil at something like £200 billion.

brief_context: The venue of the first National Energy Conference.
brief_extract: So much for EAW's contribution but should we not ask ourselves what, if anything, was gained from our participation in this day-long exercise? Firstly, we left Church House more than ever sure of the validity and relevance of our aims and objects in relation to future planning. Over and over again points had arisen which underlined the need for more education, better communication and an inexhaustible supply of public information.

brief_context: Market where New Zealand dairy produce is sold.
brief_extract:
12,000 Miles and 150 Years
by SUSAN EXCELL

The story of the New Zealand dairy industry from the early 19th century. MOST of you will have seen New Zealand butter and cheese in the shops with the familiar red and green "Anchor" emblem on the wrapper, but have you ever wondered how a country more than 12,000 miles away from Britain can send such large amounts of dairy produce to the United Kingdom and still sell it in perfect condition and at competitive prices? The story began well over 100 years ago when the first shipment of dairy produce arrived in Britain from New Zealand.

location_standardised: East India Dock, London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Arrival point for the first refrigerated shipment in 1882.
brief_extract: Unfortunately dairy produce in those days was sent as part of the general cargo of wool and tallow, and very little arrived still in good condition. The real breakthrough came in 1882 when the "Dunedin", a full-rigged sailing ship, which had set sail from New Zealand three months before, arrived at the East India Dock, with New Zealand's first refrigerated shipment of butter and cheese to Britain. This particular venture was very successful and began the real development of New Zealand's dairy industry—leading to the time when New Zealand became not only Britain's biggest supplier of butter and cheese but also the world's largest supplier of dairy produce.

brief_context: City near where Samuel Marsden established a mission.
brief_extract:
This particular venture was very successful and began the real development of New Zealand's dairy industry—leading to the time when New Zealand became not only Britain's biggest supplier of butter and cheese but also the world's largest supplier of dairy produce. It Started in 1814
However, the true origins of the New Zealand dairy industry go back long before 1882, in fact to 1814, when a certain Reverend Samuel Marsden from Britain arrived in New Zealand to establish a mission north of Auckland. He brought with him two cows and a bull — the first dairy cattle to settle in New Zealand.

brief_context: Region in New Zealand where Mr Hulke lived.
brief_extract: He brought with him two cows and a bull — the first dairy cattle to settle in New Zealand. After organised colonisation began in 1840 more cattle were imported and although the first Jersey cattle set foot in New Zealand in 1862, it was not till 1876 that real interest was shown in this particular breed when a Mr Hulke bought a young Jersey calf called Jenny in a sale, put a halter on her and walked her on foot to his home 130 miles away in Taranaki. He could not possibly have foreseen what a buy he had made as he trudged all those miles.

brief_extract: Foreign butter has always played an important part in supplies to the British market and traditionally New Zealand has been its biggest supplier. Today Britain imports three quarters of New Zealand's total butter production and a quarter of its cheese production, although for many years virtually all New Zealand's butter and cheese was exported to the United Kingdom. brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL ASSOCIATION FOR WOMEN
at 25 Foubert's Place
The long hot summer has brought many enquirers to the EAW's door, some of them tourists in London armed with maps but seeking further aid in direction finding, others intending to holiday abroad and wanting to know whether they could use their hair dryers and hair rollers in view of different European voltages and different types of plug. The heat wave produced a dramatic increase in the number of enquiries regarding refrigerators and freezers.

brief_context: A Consumer Advice Centre from here visited the EAW.
brief_extract: How to make the best economies in the use of electrical equipment is occupying most people's attention and many callers wanted specific guidance. Information is given to individuals and to groups, and a number of staff from an Essex Consumer Advice Centre spent a day in the EAW Home Economics Department using a range of domestic electrical appliances on which their advice will be sought by the public later. Visitors to EAW Headquarters included a party of women from the Finnish electrical industry who were especially interested in the EAW work with consumers and with schools.

brief_context: Mention of mandatory colour coding for domestic electrical flexibles.
brief_extract: The BSI is a member of the International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO), The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) and the European standards organisations (CEN and CENELEC). An easy example of international cooperation known to all householders is the agreement by the countries of Europe on colour coding for domestic electrical flexibles and this became mandatory in the UK from April 1971. At the Hemel Hempstead Centre of the BSI the test laboratories carry out the tests required for the British Standards and also undertake work for manufacturers throughout the world who want independent reports on the standards of their products.

brief_context: Mention of companies exporting to Canada needing certification.
brief_extract:
Standards aid exports
Successful exporters need a complete and up to date knowledge of the multitude of regulations, standards, codes of practice, approval and certification procedures and enforcing organisations throughout the world and this is provided on subscription through the Technical Help to Exporters (THE) scheme based at Hemel Hempstead. Companies exporting to Canada need certification of the Canadian Standards Association (CSA) for electrical goods and BSI acts as an agent for CSA testing to Canadian standards. This saves time and money for British businessmen.

brief_context: Home of a large supplier of bulb catalogues.

Bulb orders should have
been sent off early so that planting can take
place, if possible, at the same time as the spring
bedding plants. For a number of years I have
had catalogues sent by a large supplier in
Lincolnshire who I always believed offered

more expensive firm.

brief_extract: While this ever increasing demand, both by industrial and domestic users, for electricity at the cheapest possible rate is constantly monitored, the preservation of the countryside is always to the forefront, as evidenced by the development of the Supergrid. Members were given an opportunity to ask questions before visiting the Control rooms which, with the wall maps looking something like the London Underground routes, are the vital centres of distribution and contact with the power stations. Twenty-four hours a day manning keeps an ever-ready supply of power at the touch of a switch in homes, factories and countless other places.

brief_context: Country where the electrically driven printing presses were made.
brief_extract: This gave us a better understanding of the work being carried out in the various rooms which we toured. We were all most interested in the complicated and intricate machinery and were pleased to learn that the electrically driven presses were made in Britain by the Crabtree Vickers Engineering Group. These presses, 3 storeys high, are the first of a new and advanced design to be operated in Europe and are capable of printing 280,000 newspapers an hour.

brief_extract:
Home Economists
in Canada

Observations by three UK delegates on the XIIIth International Congress on Home Economics Ottawa, July 1976. SARAH BAILEY
MARGARET MACAULAY
NORAH RIDDINGTON

Norah Riddington, 3rd up from left; next to her Margaret Macaulay and next to her Sarah Bailey, both without glasses.

brief_context: City visited by delegates to study electricity and appliances.
brief_extract:
THE three delegates were among the 1,000 home economists from 53 countries assembled in Ottawa for the week-long congress sessions. They then spent a week in Toronto gaining an appreciation of the generation of electricity and the production, testing, selling and servicing of appliances, and an appraisal of the user information available on energy conservation. The Congress
The congress sessions were divided into the three categories of consumption, conservation and change.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding energy resources and consumption statistics.

The Congress
The congress sessions were divided into the three categories of consumption, conservation and change. Delegates were told that Europe and the USA have between them only 10% of the world's energy resources and consume 80%. There should be international unity to help solve the energy problem and people must be educated to use their resources properly.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the 'Living Standards' exhibition organized by BSI
brief_extract:
75 YEARS OF STANDARDS
THE British Standards Institution recently celebrated its 75th anniversary and as part of a campaign to show industry and the public how greatly standards contribute to a better and safer life for everyone BSI collaborated with the Design Council in arranging an exhibition at the Design Centre entitled 'Living Standards'. The exhibition gave a graphic summary of the wide range of BSI activities in the preparation and publication of the 7,000 current British Standards, and in testing services and approval procedures for goods allowed to carry the well known Kitemark and the recently introduced Safety Mark.

brief_context: Mentioned in context of export based economic recovery
brief_extract:
Said the BSI 'If you boiled a kettle for breakfast this morning, locked the front door when you left the house, walked under a street lamp on your way to work or belted yourself into your motor car for the drive to the office, you have already benefited from British Standards'. Standards and Exports
In a foreword to the BSI Annual Report the President, Baroness Seear, stressed the vital contribution which standards can make to Britain's export based economic recovery. Export trade requirements are now the major concern of BSI's technical committee work and in the international and European standards worlds BSI continues to play a leading role to the benefit of British industry and ultimately the country as a whole.

brief_context: The author and his wife holidayed in Canada.
brief_extract: The half-a-dozen were planted out. Those in pots were watered at least daily, depending on the weather, but the six planted out were only watered daily for the first six weeks and then weekly until my wife and I went to Canada for a holiday for five weeks, during which time they had no water at all. The interesting fact is that, with the exception of one shrub, not only have all survived but have made new growth as well.

brief_context: The author visited a rose nursery in this region.
brief_extract:
If you are thinking of ordering roses, unless it is absolutely necessary, you would be advised to wait until next autumn. I visited a well known rose nursery in the Midlands last September and they were very unhappy because their rose fields were parched yet they could not get permission from the Local Water Authority to irrigate. Lawns
Lawns will most certainly have suffered severely but should by now have partially recovered.

brief_context: Hanging baskets are becoming very popular there.
brief_extract:
Every few months a
recuperative period in the greenhouse would be
beneficial. Hederas (ivies) are always welcome
since they seem to survive in almost any
situation; they are ideal for hanging baskets,
which incidentally are becoming very popular in
Canada. In one nursery I visited I saw hundreds
of them planted mainly with ferns and hedera
helix (the small leaved variety) and a most
attractive show they would make in any living
room.
